'''Delbert Ray Fulkerson''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|f|ʌ|l|k|ər|s|ən}}; August 14, 1924 – January 10, 1976) was an American [[mathematician]] who co-developed the [[Ford{{Ndash}}Fulkerson algorithm]], one of the best-known [[algorithm|algorithms]] for solving the [[maximum flow problem]] in [[Flow network|network]]s.

==Early life and education==
D. R. Fulkerson was born in [[Tamms, Illinois]], the third of six children of Elbert and Emma Fulkerson. Fulkerson became an undergraduate at [[Southern Illinois University]]. His academic career was interrupted by military service during [[World War II]]. Having returned to complete his degree after the war, he went on to do a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in mathematics at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] under the supervision of [[Cyrus Colton MacDuffee|Cyrus MacDuffee]], who was a student of [[L. E. Dickson]]. Fulkerson received his Ph.D. in 1951.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecommons.library.cornell.edu/bitstream/1813/17887/2/Fulkerson_Delbert_Ray_1976.pdf|title=Delbert Ray Fulkerson|publisher=library.cornell.edu|accessdate=2014-07-01}}</ref>

==Career==
After graduation, Fulkerson joined the mathematics department at the [[RAND Corporation]]. In 1956, he and [[L. R. Ford Jr.]] described the [[Ford–Fulkerson algorithm]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ford | first1 = L. R. Jr.
 | last2 = Fulkerson | first2 = D. R.
 | mr = 0079251
 | journal = [[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]]
 | pages = 399–404
 | title = Maximal flow through a network
 | url = http://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/lans/readings/routing/ford-max_flow-1956.pdf
 | volume = 8
 | year = 1956
 | doi=10.4153/cjm-1956-045-5| s2cid = 16109790
 }}.</ref> In 1962 they produced a book-length description of their method.<ref>{{cite book
 | author1 = L. R. Ford
 | author2=D. R. Fulkerson
 | year = 1962
 | title = Flows in Networks
 | url = https://archive.org/details/flowsinnetworks0000ford
 | url-access = registration
 | publisher = Princeton University Press
 | location = Princeton, NJ
 | isbn=9780691079622
 }}</ref>

In 1971 he moved to [[Cornell University]] as the Maxwell Upson Professor of Engineering. He was diagnosed with [[Crohn's disease]] and was limited in his teaching. In despair, he committed suicide in 1976.<ref>[https://www.informs.org/Explore/History-of-O.R.-Excellence/Biographical-Profiles/Fulkerson-D.-Ray D. Ray Fulkerson] from informs.org</ref>

Fulkerson was the supervisor of [[Jon Folkman]] at RAND and [[Tatsuo Oyama]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.grips.ac.jp/list/en/facultyinfo/oyama_tatsuo/|title = OYAMA, Tatsuo &#124; GRIPS Faculty Directory}}</ref> at [[National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies|GRIPS]]. After Folkman committed suicide in 1969, Fulkerson blamed himself for failing to notice Folkman's suicidal behaviors.<ref name="Erdos">{{citation |title=The Man Who Loved Only Numbers: The Story of Paul Erdős and the Search for Mathematical Truth |first=Paul |last=Hoffman |publisher=Hyperion |year=1998 |isbn=978-0-7868-6362-4 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/manwholovedonlyn00hoff/page/109 109–110] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/manwholovedonlyn00hoff/page/109 }}.</ref>

In 1979, the [[Mathematical Programming Society]] and the [[American Mathematical Society]] established the [[Fulkerson Prize]], which is now awarded every three years for outstanding papers in [[discrete mathematics]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/prizes-awards/paview.cgi?parent_id=17 Delbert Ray Fulkerson Prize (AMS—MOS)] @ [[American Mathematical Society]]</ref>
